Name Standardizing¶

In [112]:
# making function to strip names so that difference in capitlization, spacing, and , 
# will not cause names to not match.  
def clean_name(s):
    return re.sub(r"[^a-z0-9]", "", str(s).lower())
In [113]:
# Running Data Through Function
pest_use["name_clean"]   = pest_use["COMPOUND"].map(clean_name)
pest_water["name_clean"] = pest_water["Pesticide_Name"].map(clean_name)

Getting Counties from Lat Long Values¶

In [118]:
# Load a file of county boundries in 2017
counties = gpd.read_file(
    "https://www2.census.gov/geo/tiger/GENZ2017/shp/cb_2017_us_county_500k.zip"
)[['GEOID', 'STATEFP', 'COUNTYFP', 'NAME', 'geometry']]

# Plots points and then sees which county falls into and adds column with FIPS code falls into 
sites_gdf = gpd.GeoDataFrame(
    pest_water_loc,
    geometry=gpd.points_from_xy(pest_water_loc['dec_long_va'], pest_water_loc['dec_lat_va']),
    crs="EPSG:4269"  
).to_crs(counties.crs)

#Joins dataset back with pest_water_loc
pest_water_loc = (
    gpd.sjoin(sites_gdf, counties, how='left', predicate='within')
    .rename(columns={'GEOID': 'county_fips', 'NAME': 'county_name'})
    .drop(columns=['STATEFP','COUNTYFP',"index_right"])
)

def add_zero(code):
    code = str(code)
    if len(code) < 5:
        code = '0' + code
    return code

pest_use['county_fips'] = pest_use['county_fips'].astype(int).apply(add_zero)

County Pesticide Use vs. Detected Water Concentration scatterplot.¶

According to the figure, there does not seem to be a strong (visual) relationship between pesticide use and detected water concentration, which brings into question if the data is skewed. A quality/limitation to consider is intensity of agriculture within the county, and if their pesticide use is being accurately reported (our dataset contains estimated use).

We might consider combining pesticides into use category (fungicide/herbicide/etc) for further analysis.

Data Quality Audit¶

Pest_Water¶

  • This dataset provides information on pesticide presence in streams from 2013-2022. Some results were missing detection condition, but are unimportant for our analysis goals. There is still a result value (measured in ug/L) for each location. The concentrations of pesticides in the stream seem feasible, with no values reported below 0 and 165 result reported above 10 (ug). To clean this dataset, 4 columns were kept: pesticide site (a combination of pesticide and location identifier code), pesticide name, year, and result value (concentration) Pesticide names were standardized to allow for joining with the county agricultural pesticide data. A site ID column was created from the pesticide site column, removing the pesticide name and keeping the ID code, so that the water pesticide data could be joined to the site info..

Pest_Use¶

  • This dataset provides information on estimated range of pesticides used on county-level from 2013-2017. Some results (32%) missing from low estimated use. Data set authors listed in their metadata that low estimates were missing in the data set due to either pesticide NOT being reported as unused or it was not used, but high values were always able to be calculated. For the highest end range of pesticide use, all values seem feasible, with no values below zero. To clean this dataset, 5 columns were kept: compound, year, state fips code, county fips code, and the high estimation of pesticide use. Compound names were standardized to allow for joining with the water data. The county and state fips columns were combined into one column, following the format “53005” where the first two digits are the state and the remainder represent county, in order to be able to join with the site info data.

Site_Info¶

  • This dataset gives us the physical location (lat/long) of each stream monitoring site and the location identifier code, allowing the Pest_Use and Pest_Water datasets to be joined. Some entries (2.43%) are missing from the drainage area column but that column is not pertinent to our current analyses goals. To clean this dataset, 7 columns were kept: location identifier, station name, state code, HUC, drainage area, latitude, and longitude. A site ID column was created from the location identifier, removing “USGS-” and keeping the ID code so that the site info could be joined to the water data.

Joined Data¶

  • Pest_Water was joined to Site_Info through the created site ID column. There were no rows without a matching site, and all 955,728 rows from the water data remained in the combined dataset.
  • A spatial dataset of counties (with counties selected where each of the lat/long coordinate points in the combined Pest_Water/Site_Info data) was also joined to the Pest_Water/Site_Info, adding a column for its state/county FIPS code.
  • Pest_Water/Site_Info combined dataset was joined to the Pest_Use data through county FIPS code, year, and standardized compound/pesticide name, creating a dataset with 176,787 rows that represent 74 counties. Not all counties represented in the Pest_Water dataset (82 monitoring stations) had reported agricultural pesticide use, and years were limited to 2013-2017, which is why there was a reduction in data.

Milestone 3 - Interpretation & Initial Analytical Application¶

The above figures (until the Data Quality Audit) address the following:

Question: Do regions with higher pesticide use have higher contamination concentrations in surface water?

To address this question, we plotted estimated pesticide use (kg) by measured pesticide concentrations (μg/L) in surface waters. We initially plotted the raw values, then reproduced the plot with the estimated pesticide use on a log scale, and finally reproduced the plot with both the pesticide usage and contaminant concentrations on a log scale. This final transformation revealed a more apparent trend in the data, suggesting that pesticide contaminant concentrations increase with pesticide usage. A limitation of this figure is that it does not give any information about the pesticide categories.

To begin our initial analytical approach, we created a linear regression model. We felt that this approach was best suited for our data, as we are investigating the relationship between two variables. The visual representation of a linear regression clearly asserts whether or not a trend exists within the data, and can be supported with additional statistics. In this case, we are using the R2 and p-value to determine the strength of the hypothesized relationship. A p-value of <0.001 suggests that there is some correlation between pesticide usage and contamination. An R2 value of 0.14 indicates that county pesticide usage explains 14% of the variation in pesticide concentrations in surface waters. While this suggests that a majority of the variation in surface waters is driven by other factors, such as rainfall, watershed, topography, soil characteristics, etc., it does account for a portion of the contamination variation.

Non Avg Data¶

This was done before figuring out that there were multiple measurements for stream pesticide concentration at each location, which needed to be aggregated to match the extent of the county pesticide estimate (one per year per pesticide per site).

Cloropleth Map¶

In [141]:
county_use = (
    pest_water_use
    .drop_duplicates(['county_fips', 'COMPOUND', 'Water_Year'])
    .groupby(['county_fips', 'Water_Year'])['EPEST_HIGH_KG'].sum()
    .groupby('county_fips').mean()
    .rename('pest_kg')
)

<matplotlib.legend.Legend at 0x145d437d0>

Interpretation: The point of this map was to see where the counties we are doing data anyalsis are located. It was also to see where water samples are actually collected in the county. The amount of pestcide use was taken as an average of all pestcides used and logged to be able to more easily see a difference. This data shows wide variety across the US. The water samples are collected at multiple different locations throughout teh county.

# nevermind it should be a function...

def get_pesticides(pesticide_type):
    url = f"https://www.bcpcpesticidecompendium.org/class_{pesticide_type}.html"
    response = requests.get(url)
    response.raise_for_status()
    the_website = BeautifulSoup(response.text, "html.parser")

    pesticides = [entry.get_text(strip = True) for entry in the_website.select("li a") if entry.get_text(strip = True)]

    return pesticides

Milestone 3 - Interpretation & Initial Analytical Application¶

The above pesticide category analysis plots address the following:

Question: Are there stronger correlations of pesticide use and contamination among different pesticide categories (herbicides, fungicides, insecticides, etc.)?

To address this question, we first investigated the frequency of use of each pesticide category, then compared the usage vs. contaminant concentration. The x-axis of the bar graph lists the pesticide category while the y-axis is a count of how frequently that pesticide occurred in our data set. While this visualization suggests that herbicides are used more frequently than the other pesticides, a limitation of this graph is the fact that it does not reveal information about the mass of pesticide used, which could be misleading.

The categorized plot compares the relationships between estimated usage (kg) and water contamination (μg/L) of each pesticide category. This visualization is not very informative and is limited by the sheer amount of data present. To further investigate this, we plan to average the data by county (rather than individual sample collection sites) and group by each year to reduce the volume of data being displayed.

Milestone 3 - Interpretation¶

Question: How has pesticide use and cumulative pesticide contamination changed over time?

To begin investigating this question, we plotted the frequency of occurrences within each pesticide category in our dataset from 2013 to 2017. To further explore the potential relationship between pesticide use and contamination, we plan to plot the total estimated mass of pesticides used in each category per year, along with the average contaminant concentration for each category per year. While the previous figures examine whether a relationship exists between pesticide use and contamination, analyzing how these variables change over time may provide additional evidence of a potential association. However, an important limitation of this investigation is the previously calculated R² value, which indicates that pesticide usage explains only 14% of the variation in contaminant concentrations. Although the proposed plots may reveal apparent trends or associations, they may visually suggest a stronger relationship than the data actually supports.

Milestone 3¶

Refined Questions¶

Central Question: Do regions with higher pesticide use have higher contamination concentrations in surface water?

  • Variables: Pesticide name, estimated (high) pesticide use, county fips, data collection year, pesticide water concentration
  • Observations: Our initial analysis compared pesticide use (by compound) to pesticide contamination. This relationship did not reveal a strong correlation
  • Intended comparisons: To further refine this
    • We are going to play around with log scaling the axes to see if this helps reveal a relationship
    • We are going to categorize the pesticides (herbicide, fungicide, insecticide, etc.) to see if there is greater correlation for specific compounds.
    • We are going to look at total pesticide use and total pesticide contamination (all compounds)
  • Limitations:
    • Uncertainty in the relationship between use and contamination within a county.
    • Without insight into watershed behavior, we cannot be certain that pesticides that are used within one county will contaminate the waters within that same county.

Supporting Questions:

  • Are there stronger correlations of pesticide use and contamination among different pesticide categories (herbicides, fungicides, insecticides, etc.)?
    • Variables: Pesticide category, estimated (high) pesticide use, county fips, data collection year, pesticide water concentration
    • Intended comparisons: Compare pesticide category use by pesticide category contamination
    • Limitations: We need to figure out how to group our current pesticide data measurements into their respective categories.
  • How has pesticide use and average pesticide contamination changed over time?
    • Variables: Pesticide category, estimated (high) pesticide use, county fips, data collection year, pesticide water concentration
    • Intended comparisons:
      • Compare total pesticide use for each year (2013-2017)
      • Compare average contamination concentration for each year (2013-2017)

Exploratory evidence and analytical application are addressed in the code above (Milestone 3 progress begins after Data Quality Audit)
